title: Funeral parades and seeing young Joe Oliver
summary: His cook took him to second-line funeral parades from the Washington Avenue cemetery. There he was drawn to the young cornetist Joe Oliver, who worked as a yard man. Russell adds where Oliver lived.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: And the parades, which started usually from the Bulls, that's my memory that they started there. They would always pass Terrell's Grocery on First Street, which was two or three blocks back of our house on First. And my cook always took me there to see the funerals. And we'd second line, I'd walk right along with the gang. And that is my first exposure. It was confusing to me, but it was thrilling. I enjoyed it. Maybe it was because the uniforms were gaudy. But at the time, I felt very much drawn to this youngster who was playing the cornet at the time. It was Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver. Yeah. And he worked in the neighborhood. My memory is that he was somebody's yard man between camp and magazine in that neighborhood, on First or Third. I can't pin it down any closer than that.

I think it was on Second. At least two or three people told me, Second and Magazine. And I took pictures of all four corners on there. I once took a picture of what I thought would be the building and showed it to Bunk. Bunk said, that's not it. Bunk used to go there and steal music from him, they said.
So Bunk was dead before I took the other three corners, but Louie Kepard, who I think would, who worked with Oliver at that same period. Uh-huh.
